title: Davenant: lean-on-Mediator fiducia justifies — felt assurance is its daughter
source_text: L. Sed haec de Amesio satis. Ad cujus sententiam accedit Davenantius Episcopus Sarisburiensis, qui Dordracenae Synodi pars fuit. Nam, inquit, fiducia vocabulum duo designat. Ipsum actum innitendi & adhaerendi Jesu Christo, quo quasi ambabus ulnis Christum amplectimur, & per eum actum veniam, gratiam, & gloriam conamur obtinere a Deo Patre: atque hunc putamus esse illum actum, ad quem semper sequitur justificatio, id est, absolutio a peccatis, & acceptatio in gratiam favoremque divinum; sive peccator ab ipso primo momento, animo concipiat obtentam remissionem, sive non. Solet etiam aliquando fiducia denotare consequens effectum fidei justificantis, nempe plenam persuasionem, & quasi vividum sensum remissionis impetratae, & obtenti favoris divini. Fatemur hanc fiduciam non esse fidem justificantem, sed fidei justificantis filiam; quam anima justificata, nonnisi post multa fidei & sanctitatis exercitia solet eniti. Concludimus ergo fiduciam illam in Mediatorem a Deo constitutum, nobisque in Evangelio propositum, esse illum actum cui Deus remissionem peccatorum, sive justificationem peccatoris dignatur indulgere. In libro cui titulus est, Determinationes quarundam quaestionum Theologicarum, quaest. 37. Et in quaestionis ejusdem principio docet proprium & formalem actum fidei quae justificat esse illum quo peccator promissionem salutis in Christo omni credenti factam apprehendit, & in hunc Mediatorem toto corde pro eadem obtinenda fiducialiter recumbit: Atque ut rem magis illustraret, ostendit fidei actum, quem semper & immediate sequitur justificatio, non esse nudam notitiam verbi divini: nec assensum generalem, quo agnoscimus & admittimus pro veritate divinitus revelata quicquid traditum est in Scripturis: nec etiam gratuitarum promissionum apprehensionem conditionalem: illis quidem actibus, qui communes sunt resipiscentibus & impoenitentibus, homines parari ad justificationem recipiendam: Sed descriptam fiduciam, perquam peccator in oblatum sibi Mediatorem recumbit, & illi innititur, ac divinae misericordiae se justificandum subjicit, esse ultimum illum actum cujus praesentiam ipsa justificatio concomitatur.
pass_a_gloss: But enough of Ames. To whose opinion agrees Davenant, Bishop of Salisbury, who was part of the Synod of Dort. For, he says, the word trust designates two things. The very act of leaning on and adhering to Jesus Christ, by which as with both arms we embrace Christ, and through that act we endeavor to obtain pardon, grace, and glory from God the Father: and this we think to be that act which justification always follows — that is, absolution from sins, and acceptance into divine grace and favor — whether or not the sinner from the first moment conceives in his mind that remission has been obtained. Trust is also sometimes wont to denote the consequent effect of justifying faith, namely a full persuasion, and as it were a vivid sense of remission obtained, and of divine favor gotten. We confess that this trust is not justifying faith, but the daughter of justifying faith; which a justified soul is wont to bring forth only after many exercises of faith and holiness. We conclude therefore that that trust in the Mediator constituted by God and set before us in the Gospel is that act to which God deigns to grant remission of sins, or the justification of the sinner. In the book titled Determinations of certain Theological Questions, question 37. And at the beginning of the same question he teaches that the proper and formal act of the faith which justifies is that by which the sinner apprehends the promise of salvation in Christ made to every believer, and fiducially reclines with whole heart upon this Mediator for obtaining the same: And that he might illustrate the matter more, he shows that the act of faith which justification always and immediately follows is not bare knowledge of the divine word: nor general assent by which we acknowledge and admit as truth divinely revealed whatever is handed down in the Scriptures: nor even a conditional apprehension of free promises: by those acts indeed, which are common to the penitent and the impenitent, men are prepared to receive justification: But the described trust, by which the sinner reclines upon the Mediator offered to him, and leans on Him, and subjects himself to the divine mercy to be justified, is that last act whose presence justification itself accompanies.
pass_b_english: 1. Lean-on/embrace-Christ act — justification always follows, with or without felt remission at once.
2. Full vivid sense of obtained remission/favor — daughter of justifying faith, after exercises.
Proper formal act: apprehend the promise and fiducially rest on the Mediator.
Not bare notitia, general assent, or mere conditional promise-grasp — those prepare; lean-on-Mediator is the last accompanying act.
